To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Eastern Enlargements had a negative effect, that is, the Enlargement led to lower employment growth in German firms.

the Eastern Enlargements had a negative effect of employment growth in German establishments, that this effect is driven by increased separation and destruction of jobs, and that the effect is more negative for low- and mediumskilled workers than for high-skilled workers.

the Eastern Enlargements had an overall negative employment effect that was driven by increased worker separation and increased job destruction, and that there is a clear indication for a skill-bias in the employment effect.

the effects of an increase of trade liberalisation in a context of an enlarged market, and the effects on employment.
the question whether the Eastern Enlargements of the European Union had a positive or negative effect on employment.
the question of how a trade liberalisation shock affects the employment of workers.

there is a skill bias in employment effects of the Eastern En largement.
the Enlargements effect is skill biased and that the skill bias is driven by the negative employment effects on low- and medium- skilled workers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Eastern Enlargements of the European Union in 2004 and 2007 had a negative employment effect on German establishments.
the Enlargements effects are heterogeneous across skill groups of the labour force.
the Enlargements’ effect on employment is negative, driven by an increase in job destruction and worker separations, and that this effect is skill biased.

an increase in trade induced demand shock can have significant negative effects on employment, especially on low-skilled workers.
